You use present perfect continuous to talk about actions that started in the past and continue to happen in the present in a progressive way.

Whenever we want to express that we started an action, and that we are still doing it, we can use present perfect continuous. In order to formulate sentences, we are always going to use the verb in past participle been after have or has.

Let's review the grammatical structure:

Subject + have/has + been + (verb + ing) + complement


Example:
Clouds have been giving users big amount of space for storage.
My flash drive has been showing some error messages.
These kind of devices have been evolving to give us the space for storage that we need.
Storage in the cloud has been becoming more popular.
Solid-state and storage in the cloud have been helping users to back up and maintain information accessible.
You use simple present passive in affirmative, negative and questions to provide more importance to the object and the action in a sentence rather than the subject.
Solid-state storage is reflected on most portable devices that we use nowadays.
Our files aren't limited to only one device as they will be part of a remote server.
How are clouds composed and what are they used for?

When we use passive voice, we focus on the object of the action rather than on the subject. The subject can be mentioned or omitted and the sentence should keep the same intention. If you want to mention the subject, you use by after the verb.

Let's review the grammatical structure in affirmative, negative and interrogative sentences.

Affirmative:
Object of the sentence + verb to be + verb in past participle + Complement


Example: Flash drives are used (by people) to transport data easily.

Negative:
Object of the sentence + (verb to be + not) + verb in past participle + Complement


Example: Clouds aren't used (by people) as frequently as flash drives.

Questions:
Verb to be + object of the sentence + verb in past participle + Complement +?


Example: Are clouds designed to upload any kind of file?

As you can see in the examples, the object is more important than the subject.

images.text:
Lesley: Welcome to “Radio Computer”...

We are going to analyze some written information about solid-state storage and storage in the cloud by the systems engineer Thomas Smith. According to him, solid-state storage is reflected on most portable devices that we use nowadays. Flash drives, memory sticks or portable devices with built-in memory are some examples of solid-state storage. These kinds of devices have been evolving to give us the space for storage that we need. On the other hand, storage in the cloud has been becoming more popular. It is easy to find internet connections wherever we go and our files aren't limited to only one device as they will be part of a remote server. Now, we are going to answer some questions from the listeners.

The first question is: “What is a flash memory made of?” Well, a flash memory is made of a grid of cells. Each cell contains two transistors, one of them is called control gate, and this transistor is in charge of controlling the flow of charge. The other transistor is called floating gate, it is in charge of registering all the information in the device. The second question is: “How are clouds composed and what are they used for?”  The cloud service is provided through a network. They aren't designed only to back up information, the idea is for you to have access to your files and share them anywhere you are.

To conclude this show, I will read a summary that one of the listeners wrote… Solid-state and storage in the cloud have been helping users to back up and maintain information accessible. Clouds have been changing the way in which we share information, and USBs allow us to carry files without the necessity of an internet connection. They're a good complement.
